title: Fundamentals of Travel and Tourism Geography
summary: All travel is not tourism: travel is any journey, tourism is travel for leisure, recreation, enjoyment or rejuvenation. Geography helps tourism by locating a place on the globe or map, finding the time-lag between origin and destination, setting the clock, showing data through maps and charts and by explaining transport, distance, site and location, and the environmental conditions of a destination.

Latitude is the angular distance north or south of the equator (0° to 90° N and 0° to 90° S). Latitudes run east-west, are parallel (parallels) and are complete circles that get smaller towards the poles. The equator is the only latitude whose plane passes through the centre of the earth, so it is a great circle and the shortest distance along it is the shortest path.

Longitude is the angular distance east or west of the prime meridian (0°, through Greenwich near London), numbered 0° to 180° E and 0° to 180° W. Lines of longitude (meridians) run from the North Pole to the South Pole, are not parallel, are half circles, cut the latitudes at 90° and are closer together towards the poles. The prime meridian and 180° divide the earth into the eastern and western hemispheres; the equator divides it into the northern and southern hemispheres. India lies in the northern and eastern hemispheres.

The earth turns 360° in 24 hours, so 15° = 1 hour and 1° = 4 minutes. The standard time of a country is taken from its central meridian. India extends from 68° E to 97° E and its central meridian is 82°30' E (near Naini, Allahabad), so IST is 82.5 × 4 = 330 minutes = 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of Greenwich Mean Time. The local time difference between the east and west ends of India is about two hours. Large countries have several time zones: Australia 3, mainland USA 4, Canada 6, Russia 9. Tourists must adjust their watches and may suffer sleep disorder (jet lag), especially on east-west journeys.

To calculate time: find the longitude difference (subtract if both are on the same side of 0°, add if on opposite sides), multiply by 4 for minutes and divide by 60 for hours. Add the difference when going east (east is ahead) and subtract when going west. Example: 45° E at 8 am and 120° E: difference 75°, 75 × 4 = 300 minutes = 5 hours, so it is 1 pm at 120° E.

The International Date Line is an imaginary line from the North Pole to the South Pole that separates one calendar day from the next. It follows 180° longitude roughly down the middle of the Pacific Ocean and bends around the Far East of Russia and island groups. Crossing it from west to east (eastbound) takes away one day (the date repeats); crossing it from east to west (westbound) adds a day.

Maps are of two kinds: general reference maps (world, countries, rivers, mountains; collected in an atlas) and special or thematic maps (climate, vegetation, rainfall, crops, minerals, roads, railways, air routes). Features of thematic maps useful to tourists: the political map shows boundaries, capitals, cities, ports, roads and railways; the physical map shows elevation by shades (darker for higher); the road map shows roads, petrol pumps and lodging and the distance matrix; the railway map shows gauge, route length, electrified or diesel sections and tracks; the air route map shows airports and routes; the tourist map shows scenic spots, hill stations, monuments, religious places, beaches and sanctuaries; the trekking route map shows paths, heights, camp sites, rivers and mountains. To read a map, check latitude and longitude, the scale, direction and legend.
Charts: a bar chart compares categories, a line chart shows a trend over time, a pie chart shows proportionate shares of a whole (100%); others are scatter diagrams, histograms and flow charts.

objective: Fill in the blanks. (a) ________ is used to study the trend of any phenomenon over a certain time period. (b) India's time is decided by the longitude value of ________.
(a) A line chart. (b) 82°30' E (the central meridian near Naini, Allahabad).
State whether True or False. (a) The prime meridian divides the earth into two hemispheres. (b) All lines of longitude cut the lines of latitude at 90°.
State whether True or False. (a) All lines of longitude cut lines of latitude at 90°. (b) Canada has three time zones.
(a) True. (b) False: Canada has six time zones (Australia has three).
Fill in the blanks. (a) The latitude that passes through the centre of the earth is called the ________. (b) The line passing through 0° passes through ________ near London.
Fill in the blanks. (a) From the equator to the North Pole, the area is called the ________ hemisphere. (b) The earth rotates on its axis once in ________ hours.
State whether True or False. (a) The longitudinal extent of India is 68° to 97° West. (b) The local time difference between the easternmost and westernmost points of India is about two hours.
(a) False: it is 68° E to 97° E. (b) True.
State whether True or False. (a) India has two time zones. (b) To find the time difference between two places it is enough to know the longitude of one place.
(a) False: India follows one standard time (IST). (b) False: the longitudes of both places are needed.

vsa: Describe any two features of a General Reference Map.

It gives general information about spatial units such as the world, continents, countries, districts, cities, rivers, mountains and oceans. It is found in books and atlases, and an atlas is a collection of such maps.
April 2026

or: Describe any two features of a Political Map.
It shows international, state and coastal boundaries, state capitals, cities, ports, roads and railways. Different colours separate political units but no colour has a special meaning.

vsa: How does knowledge of geography help in tourism? Explain in two points.

It helps tourists locate a place on the globe or map and find the time-lag between origin and destination. It also gives information about transport, distances and environmental conditions, and helps in reading maps and charts.
April 2026
Describe any two geographical factors affecting tourism.

Location and climate decide the season, route and distance for a destination. Physical features (mountains, coast, deserts, rivers) and time-lag decide what a place offers and how tourists plan their travel.
October 2025
Explain the role of geography in travel and tourism.
Geography helps tourists locate places with latitude and longitude, calculate time-lag and set clocks, and read maps and charts. It also explains the climate, relief and transport of a destination.
October 2025

or: Why should travellers have basic knowledge of latitude and longitude? Explain.
They locate any place on earth precisely and help find time differences. Latitude also indicates the climate of a place.

vsa: Describe any two features of a tourist map.

It shows places of tourist interest such as scenic spots, hill stations, monuments, religious places, beaches and sanctuaries. It also shows their location in relation to rivers, lakes, mountains and forests and is prepared from national to local level.
April 2025
What is a special or thematic map? Name two thematic maps.

A special or thematic map gives specific information such as climate, rainfall, vegetation, crops, minerals, roads or railways. Examples are the road map and the railway map (also the trekking route map).
October 2025
Define the term 'thematic map'.
A thematic map is a special map that shows one theme or topic, such as climate, vegetation, rainfall, industries, roads, railways or air routes.
October 2024
What is the International Date Line? What happens when it is crossed?
It is an imaginary line along 180° longitude from pole to pole that separates one calendar day from the next. Crossing it eastbound subtracts a day and crossing westbound adds a day.
Distinguish between latitude and longitude (two points).
Latitudes run east-west, are parallel and measure distance north or south of the equator; longitudes run from pole to pole, are not parallel and measure distance east or west of the prime meridian.
sa: Describe any three features of a trekking route map.

(i) It shows the tracks in mountain areas along which trekking is possible. (ii) It shows the heights at different places and camp pitching grounds. (iii) It also shows rivers and the mountain system, helping adventure tourists plan the trek.
What are special or thematic maps? Explain any two thematic maps.

Special or thematic maps give information on a theme such as climate or roads. (i) A railway map shows gauge, route length, electrified or diesel sections and single or double track, helping tourists plan train journeys. (ii) A road map shows national and state highways, petrol pumps, lodging and the distance matrix.
How do geographical factors affect tourism? Explain.

(i) Location and distance from the source decide cost and time-lag. (ii) Climate and relief decide the season and the type of tourism, such as hill stations in summer. (iii) Natural features such as coasts, mountains and rivers form attractions.
Explain how to calculate the time at one place from the time at another, in three points.

(i) Find the longitude difference: subtract if both are on the same side of the prime meridian, add if on opposite sides. (ii) Multiply the difference by 4 to get minutes and divide by 60 for hours. (iii) Add the time difference if the other place is east and subtract if it is west.
Distinguish between a bar chart and a pie chart.

(i) A bar chart uses rectangular bars to compare values for different categories such as arrivals at centres. (ii) A pie chart is a circle divided into sectors showing each item's share of a total (100%). (iii) Bars suit comparison and pies suit proportions.
la: Explain the significance of geography for tourism in six points.

(i) It helps in locating a place with latitude and longitude. (ii) It helps calculate the time-lag between source and destination. (iii) It helps set the time of a clock in a global context and adjust for the date line. (iv) Maps and charts show facts about places, transport and distances. (v) It explains the environment, climate and relief of the destination so that seasons can be chosen. (vi) It helps tourists understand and read different maps, such as political, road, railway and tourist maps.
Explain how a tourist can find the time difference between two places on the globe, with the effect of the International Date Line, in six points.

(i) Earth rotates 360° in 24 hours, so 15° is one hour and 1° is four minutes. (ii) Find the longitude difference by subtracting (same hemisphere) or adding (different hemispheres). (iii) Multiply by 4 for minutes and divide by 60 for hours. (iv) The time is ahead in the east, so add going east and subtract going west. (v) Example: 45° E at 8 am and 120° E gives 75° × 4 = 300 minutes = 5 hours, so 1 pm. (vi) Crossing the International Date Line (180°) eastbound reduces one day and westbound adds one day.
Explain any four thematic maps useful to tourists, in six points.

(i) Political map: boundaries, capitals, ports, roads and railways, to locate places. (ii) Physical map: relief by shades, to prepare for elevation and temperature. (iii) Road map: highways, petrol pumps and lodging, with the distance matrix. (iv) Railway map: gauge, route length and electrified or diesel lines, to plan journeys. (v) Air route map: airports and routes, to find short routes. (vi) Tourist and trekking maps: attractions, paths, heights and camp sites.
